syllabusTopics: Saturated hydrocarbons (Alkanes): preparation from haloalkanes (reduction and Wurtz reaction), decarboxylation, catalytic hydrogenation of alkene and alkyne
Chemical properties of alkanes: substitution reactions (halogenation, nitration and sulphonation only), oxidation of ethane
Unsaturated hydrocarbons (Alkenes): preparation by dehydration of alcohol, dehydrohalogenation, catalytic hydrogenation of alkyne
Chemical properties of alkenes: addition reaction with HX (Markovnikov's addition and peroxide effect), H2O, O3, H2SO4 only
Alkynes: preparation from carbon and hydrogen, 1,2-dibromoethane, chloroform/iodoform only
Chemical properties of alkynes: addition reaction with H2, HX, H2O; acidic nature (action with sodium, ammoniacal AgNO3 and ammoniacal Cu2Cl2)
Test of unsaturation (ethene and ethyne): bromine water test and Baeyer's test
Comparative studies of physical properties of alkane, alkene and alkyne
Kolbe's electrolysis methods for the preparation of alkanes, alkenes and alkynes

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — Making the π Bond Alkenes carry one C=C double bond (**CₙH₂ₙ**, sp², planar). Their preparations all create that π bond by **elimination**: water out of an alcohol (**dehydration**), HX out of a haloalkane (**dehydrohalogenation**), or H₂ off an alkyne (**catalytic hydrogenation** of the triple bond).  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts ### 2.1 Dehydration of alcohols - **C₂H₅OH → CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O** with **conc. H₂SO₄ at ~170 °C** (or Al₂O₃, ~350 °C). - Ethanol → ethene; propan-2-ol → propene. Acid-catalysed: protonate –OH, lose water, lose H⁺. - Competing substitution (ethoxyethane) at lower temperature (~140 °C) — temperature decides. ### 2.2 Dehydrohalogenation (β-elimination) - **CH₃CH₂Br + alc.…

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: H2SO4 170 °C = alkene; 140 °C = ether. alc. KOH = eliminate; aq. KOH = substitute. Lindlar = stop at alkene. Hydrogenation mechanism: adsorb → syn add → desorb.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: Elimination chemistry makes π bonds: water out (acid, 170 °C), HX out (alcoholic base), H₂ partially off an alkyne (poisoned catalyst) — three exits, one alkene.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Alkenes CnH2n, sp2 planar, one C=C. Preparation: (1) dehydration of alcohols — C2H5OH -> CH2=CH2 + H2O, conc H2SO4 ~170C or Al2O3 ~350C; 140C gives ether instead. (2) Dehydrohalogenation — CH3CH2Br + alc. KOH -> CH2=CH2 + KBr + H2O; beta-elimination; Saytzeff rule (more substituted alkene major).…

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Saytzeff's rule is stability in disguise: the more substituted double bond is the more hyperconjugation-stabilised one, so elimination votes for it.
